newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Traders rule Russia sugar as Cuba deals fade.
newsitem.headline: Traders rule Russia sugar as Cuba deals fade.

text.p: Commodity powerhouses are in the ascendency in Russia's big sugar import business as the role of unwieldy Soviet-era protocols and central planning quickly wanes, industry analysts said on Wednesday.

Once a business ruled by oil-for-sugar barters between Russia and Cuba, the trade is increasingly dominated by private firms -- domestic and foreign -- which are moving to fill the gap left by the failure of Russia and Cuba to strike a deal this year.
"The private sector is far more adept at bringing the two sides together," said Chris Pack, analyst at sugar trade house Czarnikow Sugar in London.
"I think the role of the protocols (between Cuba and Russia) is on the wane."
Russian trade houses confirmed the trend, saying that few, if any, of the country's raw sugar imports so far this year had been under government-to-government barter deals.
A 1997 Cuba-Russia protocol has yet to be negotiated, although small deliveries may have been made this year under a delayed 1996 arrangement, they said.

"I don't think there have been many deliveries at all on a government-to-government basis," said Vladimir Bjedougov, deputy director of the international department at major Russian trade house Alfa-Eko.
"Last year the protocol (with Cuba) was implemented and our company and Menatep delivered substantial (early) volumes of Cuban raws into Russia."
Traders saw Russia's sugar industry following the same path of liberalisation as the grain sector, where direct purchases by the government are already a thing of the past.
As long as Moscow could control the domestic price of sugar sold to consumers, it was less concerned about paying often wildly-inflated prices for part of its erstwhile ally Cuba's sugar cane crop.
But Moscow's influence has not been completely eclipsed by the arrival of the trading houses.
Last week it said it would slap a hefty 25 percent import duty on most refined sugar, in a move that has major repercussions for the raw sugar trade.

Russian dealers have already reported a drop in white sugar imports from other members of the Commonwealth of Independent States since the announcement, even though the duty will not be implemented until May 15.
Traders said the government had apparently succeeded in its aim to help domestic refineries by restricting the amount of cheap white sugar coming into the country.
Raw sugar needs were likely to rise as a result, analysts said.
"I would think that this duty will confirm the trend towards importing raws into Russia," Pack said.

Traders in London and Moscow said that raw sugar imports were likely to pick up sharply during the second quarter of 1997 after starting slowly in the first quarter due to low domestic prices and delays at the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
A port official said earlier that a backlog of around 140,000 tonnes of raws had built up and that it would take a month to clear it up.
Further shipments were to arrive soon through Latvia's Baltic Sea port of Riga to avoid the bottleneck, traders said.

Russia traditionally meets its annual refined sugar demand of around five million tonnes by importing whites mainly from Ukraine, refining imported raws mainly from Cuba and refining its own sugar beet crop.

But high imports of cheap Ukrainian sugar last year hit Russia's refineries hard and prompted calls for greater protection in 1997. At the end of 1996, refineries were working at an average of only 50 to 60 percent of capacity.
